source: Bizer and Petty (2005) How we conceptualize our attitudes matters (Political Psychology 26, 553-568)
finding: Founding result. The same preference framed as opposing the rejected candidate resisted a later attack message more than the same preference framed as supporting the preferred one. Study 2 said not a priming effect. Study 3 said it generalises. Baseline preference was equal in both groups.
numbers: No N or effect size seen. Full text not obtained. Secondary description: fictional election, Chris vs Rick, equal initial preference, attack message on the preferred candidate.
limits: Paper itself not read. Numbers unverified. Do not quote effect sizes for it.
agent_relevance: Reframing the same stance in negative words changes how stubborn it becomes while leaving its direction unchanged. A support/oppose wording flip could change the agent's later resistance to correction.

source: Teeny blog post summarising Bizer and Petty 2005 and Bizer, Larsen, Petty 2011
finding: Secondary account. Opposition-framed participants were less moved by an attack message. A replication with real Virginia governor voters is reported. Manipulated opposition mindset raised reported likelihood of voting. Proposed mechanism: negative features weigh more, so thinking about the rejected option's negatives strengthens the preference.
numbers: No sample sizes, statistics or effect sizes given in the post.
limits: Blog, not peer reviewed. Mechanism is the author's reading. The evolutionary talk is speculation.
agent_relevance: Mechanism is attention to the negatives of the rejected option, not an opinion change. It matters when the agent compares options.

source: Bizer, Larsen, Petty (2011) Exploring the valence-framing effect: negative framing enhances attitude strength
finding: Negative framing raised attitude certainty (Exp 1). In a representative sample of residents of two U.S. states during campaigns (Exp 2), negative framing raised certainty and attitude-consistent behavioural intentions. Certainty mediated the effect on intentions.
numbers: Two experiments. No N or effect size seen.
quote: Valence framing thus appears to be a relatively low-effort way to impact multiple features associated with strong attitudes.
limits: Abstract only (via Crossref). Framing was imposed by the experimenter, not chosen freely.
agent_relevance: Valence framing moves confidence, not only resistance. Wording should not be allowed to inflate the agent's certainty.

source: Authors unverified (2012) When are support and opposition not opposites? Depth of processing as a moderator of the valence-framing effect (Br J Soc Psychol)
finding: Replicated the effect (opposers had stronger attitudes than supporters) in three studies, but only when the attitude was personally relevant (Exp 1 and 3) and when people were not under cognitive load (Exp 2). So the effect needs deep processing.
numbers: Three experiments. Numbers not seen.
quote: but only when attitudes were relevant to the participants (Experiments 1 and 3), and when participants were not under cognitive load
limits: Boundary conditions: low personal relevance and high load abolish the effect. Abstract only, via Crossref.
agent_relevance: Strongest boundary condition. The effect needs elaboration, so an agent that thinks deeply about its stance may be more exposed than one that skims. It is not a shallow cue.

source: Rovenpor, Teeny, Petty (2023 preprint) Independents, not partisans, are more likely to hold and express electoral preferences based in negativity
finding: Independents more often frame their preference in oppositional terms and act on opposition. In Study 4 independents agreed more with negatively framed appeals, while partisans showed the opposite. Study 5 replicated the valenced pattern in three non-political domains.
numbers: Five studies, total N=51,687. Study 1 spans five decades of survey data. Study 2 covers four presidential elections.
limits: Abstract only. Studies 1 to 3 are observational. Study 4 is the experimental one. Preprint.
agent_relevance: An individual-difference moderator. Who benefits from oppositional wording depends on baseline stance, so no fixed framing choice has a universal effect.

source: Kellogg faculty listing for Petty-lab 2025 paper: when and why opposition vs support framing increases choice (web-search summary)
finding: Search summary says opposition framing strengthens attitudes and raises willingness to pay only when choosing between two options of similar extremity.
numbers: Not available.
limits: Page returned 404. Only a search snippet seen. Unconfirmed lead.
agent_relevance: If true, the effect depends on how close the options are. In close calls neutral restatement matters most.

source: Piñon and Gambara (2005) A meta-analytic review of framing effect (Psicothema 17, 325-331)
finding: 51 studies (1997 to 2003), 151 effect sizes, about 13,500 subjects. Average Cohen's d: risky-choice 0.44, goal 0.44, attribute 0.26. Heterogeneity highly significant (p<.0001).
numbers: Within attribute framing: student samples d=0.22, between-subjects d=0.24, multiple options d=0.37 vs single option d=0.19, Psychology studies d=-0.25 (no effect, wrong sign), Economics d=0.42. Attribute regression R2=0.569.
limits: Mostly gain/loss wording (94.7%). Asian disease was 47.7% of effects. Heterogeneity means no single true size. Authors note Levin et al. 1998 argued Kuhberger's earlier meta-analysis was biased.
agent_relevance: Attribute-type wording shifts are small to moderate and very task-dependent. Do not assume a fixed penalty.

source: Kühberger (2023) A systematic review of risky-choice framing effects (EXCLI J 22:1012-1031)
finding: Risky-choice framing is robust. Kuhberger 1998 meta-analysis d=0.31 (100+ studies, about 30,000 participants). Corrected for publication bias (Steiger and Kuhberger 2018) d=0.52. Many Labs risky-choice d=0.60. Im and Chen 2022 (49 countries, over 100,000 people) h=0.612, CI 0.568 to 0.656. Binomial display: d=0.60 equals 36% to 64%.
numbers: Design variation gave d=0.16 to 0.91. Asian-disease-like subset: 63% choose the sure gain vs 41% the sure loss (22 points). Facet study: about 26 percentage points on average across probabilities, formats, order and layout.
limits: No single true effect size. The reviewer argues the effects show adaptive processing, not only irrationality. Publication-bias correction went upward, so no sign of inflation.
agent_relevance: The classic gain/loss effect is real and large for humans. It is the baseline for LLM comparisons.

source: Kühberger (2023) on attribute and message framing evidence (inside the same review)
finding: Little but mostly positive evidence for attribute framing. No consistent evidence for goal or message framing. Message framing effects about d=0.10 (O'Keefe and Jensen 2008, 2009). Food meta-analysis (Dolgopolova 2021; 25 studies, 76 effects): gain frame d=0.47 overall, attitudes d=0.82, intentions d=0.05.
numbers: Florence 2022: 12 studies favoured positive, 10 negative. Ainiwaer 2021 on cancer messages mixed.
limits: Cited second-hand inside an opened review. Gain/loss message framing is not the same manipulation as support/oppose, but it is the closest meta-analytic evidence.
agent_relevance: Wording moves stated evaluation far more than downstream action. Check the agent's actions, not only its stated confidence.

source: Kühberger (2023) on age and individual differences (inside the same review)
finding: Best and Charness 2015 meta-analysis (18 studies, over 3,000 people): younger adults more risk-prone in positive frames, no age effect in negative frames. Big Five effects judged absent. Time pressure assumed to raise framing but evidence is mixed.
numbers: Age differences small at best.
limits: Second-hand within an opened review.
agent_relevance: Moderators like time pressure are weak, so framing is not just a speed error. Slowing the agent will not remove it.

source: Mandel (2020 repost of 2013 reply) On framing effects, replications, and scientific inference
finding: Replication dispute. Simmons and Nelson replicated Mandel 2014 Exp 2 (2 frame x 3 modifier: none, 'at least', 'exactly'). They found a strong framing effect even with 'exactly' (t=5.64, df=225, p<.0001). Mandel had found none (t(74)=1.37). Mandel says the percentages choosing the sure option did not differ in any cell after Bonferroni, so each cell replicated.
numbers: Heterogeneity: Simmons and Nelson 'no modifier' vs 'exactly' Q=4.15, p=.042. 'At least' vs 'exactly' Q=0.01, p=.92. No-modifier effects across the two studies Q=1.02, p=.31. Chance of a significant replication given Mandel's effect: 28.3%.
limits: mTurk vs university samples. About 50 failing a recall check were removed. The reply is by the original author, so partisan.
agent_relevance: Framing depends partly on whether numbers are read as 'exactly N' or 'at least N'. A restatement step must keep quantity wording fixed.

source: Mandel (2014) Do framing effects reveal irrational choice? (JEP General)
finding: Argues part of the classic Asian disease framing effect arises because people read unmodified numbers as 'at least'. Adding 'exactly' removed the effect in his Exp 2.
numbers: Known through Crossref, the reply above and Payne 2025. Not read in full.
limits: Failed to replicate in Simmons and Nelson 2013 (strong effect with 'exactly').
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: part of framing is interpretation of wording, not valuation. Precise neutral restatement can remove that part.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of large language models via human cognitive biases (NeurIPS)
finding: GPT-3 (davinci-002) on Asian-disease style prompts chose the risky option 11.3% under 'save' framing vs 60.0% under 'die' framing when save probability was under 0.5. Overall 45.4% vs 74.1% (human original 28% vs 78%).
numbers: Save vs die by save probability: under 0.5: 11.3 vs 60.0. At 0.5: 21.9 vs 46.9. Over 0.5: 84.4 vs 93.8.
limits: Single early base model with no instruction tuning. Prompt in the original T&K style, so memorisation is possible. Gap vanishes when the risky option is not really risky.
agent_relevance: LLMs reproduce the gain/loss flip, so the framing effect is in the model, not only in people.

source: Suri et al. (2023) Do large language models show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5
finding: ChatGPT showed a clear framing effect. Gain frame ('70 of 100 improved') gave rating 5 in all 11 trials. Loss frame ('30 did not improve') gave rating 4 in all 11. Humans (mTurk, N=82: 44 gain, 39 loss) gave 5.2 vs 4.6, t(80)=3.86, p<.001.
numbers: Model: 11 trials per frame, 22 total, zero variance. Human CIs 5.03 to 5.37 and 4.35 to 4.85.
limits: Rated efficacy, not choice, because the model would not give decisions. New window per trial. Tiny N, deterministic outputs.
agent_relevance: Identical data worded as gain gives a one-point higher rating with no noise. This is a systematic bias, not randomness, so repeat sampling will not average it away.

source: Suri et al. (2023): linguistic account of framing
finding: Authors note framing vanishes in a non-native language (Keysar and Hayakawa 2012). They propose that part of framing is linguistic association that is strongest in the native tongue, which the model shares.
numbers: No test run. Interpretation only.
limits: Speculative. Rival to the emotional-distance account.
agent_relevance: If framing is partly lexical association, a symbolic or language-neutral restatement should remove it. That is testable.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs
finding: Admissions prompts with admit vs reject framing. GPT-4 admits 40.5% more students under the reject framing. Llama 2 7B classifies 32.1% fewer females as good at math in the group-attribution test.
numbers: Self-help debiasing (model rewrites the prompt) left framing-biased prompt elements at 0% for Llama 2 13B, 1.4% for Llama 2 7B, 2.7% for GPT-4. Awareness prompting for GPT-3.5 left 17.2%. Few-shot debiasing sometimes drove admission to 0 or 1.
limits: Models: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama 2 7B and 13B. Table reports admission-rate differences. Direction is not a simple gain/loss analogue.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a neutral-restatement state. Rewriting the prompt to strip biased wording worked best. Warnings helped less. Few-shot sometimes broke the model.

source: Itzhak et al. (2023) Instructed to bias: instruction-tuned language models exhibit emergent cognitive bias
finding: Studied the decoy effect, certainty effect and belief bias. Framing itself is not tested. Reports that instruction tuning and RLHF amplify these biases relative to base models.
numbers: Framing mentioned only in passing in the text read.
limits: Listed to prevent a wrong claim: the CogBias paper groups this with framing studies.
agent_relevance: Tuned models are not safe by default from wording effects. Do not cite this paper for framing.

source: Malberg et al. (2025) A comprehensive evaluation of cognitive biases in LLMs
finding: 30 cognitive biases on 20 LLMs. Every bias appeared in at least some models. Framing Effect score averaged 0.41 (per-model range 0.10 to 0.55, random baseline 0.01). Anchoring 0.39, loss aversion 0.33, in-group 0.41, information bias 0.54.
numbers: Framing items follow the attribute-framing definition: 7-point Likert, negative framing expected to give a less favourable evaluation.
limits: Scores are normalised bias metrics, not Cohen's d. Mixed open and closed models. Synthetic prompts.
agent_relevance: LLM framing sensitivity is broad and medium in size. It appears in nearly every model, so guard against it by design.

source: Payne (2025) An analysis of AI decision under risk: prospect theory emerges in large language models
finding: Five models (GPT-4o, o3, Claude Sonnet 4 with and without thinking, Gemini 1.5 Pro), 25 iterations per condition, 2,550 decisions. Framing effect (loss-frame minus gain-frame risk score) was large in sport: GPT-4o +1.84, Gemini +1.4 (lowest). It reversed in career (GPT-4o -0.37, Gemini -0.52) and business (GPT-4o -0.20).
numbers: Framing size was not correlated with attempts at expected-value calculation. 2.3% of returns could not be parsed.
limits: Custom three-option scenarios, not standard problems. Gemini 2.5 Pro was excluded because of refusals. Sign changes with domain.
agent_relevance: The sign of the framing effect depends on the semantic domain, not just the gain/loss structure. Thinking models did not remove it.

source: Payne (2025): purely mathematical control scenarios
finding: A parallel condition gave the same payoffs in symbolic notation with no semantic content, for GPT-4o and o3, to separate wording effects from maths ability.
numbers: Two models only. Exact control numbers not recorded here.
limits: Small control. Domain wording is the active ingredient.
agent_relevance: Replacing words by symbols is a testable neutralising operator for the S1 restatement step.

source: Lior, Naccache, Stanovsky (2026) WildFrame: comparing the framing effect in humans and LLMs on naturally occurring texts
finding: 1,000 real texts reframed positively or negatively (for example adding 'although I lost all my friends'). Eleven LLMs shift sentiment like humans (r about 0.52 and up). Both humans and models are moved more by positive than negative reframing.
numbers: Correlation with humans: GPT-3.5 0.52, GPT-4o 0.57, GPT-5-mini 0.61. Instance-level sentiment changes in about 55% of cases under prompt paraphrase.
limits: A sentiment-labelling task. Framing here is an appended opposite-sentiment clause. Crowd data checked against an in-house baseline.
agent_relevance: Newer models track human framing more closely, not less. Positive reframing hits harder than negative, which cuts against the 'negativity dominates' story.

source: Yun et al. (2026) This treatment works, right? Evaluating LLM sensitivity to patient question framing in medical QA
finding: 6,614 query pairs from clinical trial abstracts, eight LLMs, retrieval-grounded. Evidence-direction agreement was 76.2% for same-framing pairs and 72.0% for positive/negative framed pairs. Logistic coefficient -0.219, SE 0.015, z=-14.72, p<.001.
numbers: Multi-turn: 78.4% baseline vs 70.7% framed. Single turn: 75.4% vs 72.4%. Effectiveness questions were most susceptible. No interaction with plain vs technical language (plain 75.5 vs 71.9; technical 76.1 vs 71.5).
limits: Eight models differ in susceptibility. Framing here is question wording (positive vs negative), the closest design to support/oppose wording.
agent_relevance: Opposite-valence question wording flips the evidence conclusion about 4 points more often, rising to about 8 under multi-turn persuasion. Direct evidence for a neutral restatement state.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: measuring and mitigating cognitive bias in LLMs
finding: Three LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B) show bias in all four families. Judgment-bias shifts were 2.7 to 7.7 percentage points. Prompt-level debiasing reduces response biases but backfires for judgment biases. Activation steering: Llama negligible degradation, Qwen up to -19.0 pp on judgment.
numbers: Order bias 30 to 66%. First-option selection 77 to 79% vs 36.8% chance.
limits: Three models, temperature 0, one benchmark. Framing is only one judgment bias and is not separated in the numbers read.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to be unbiased can make judgment bias worse. Code-level checks beat instructions, in line with G5.

source: CogBias (2026) citing Echterhoff 2024 and Itzhak 2024 on LLM framing
finding: CogBias says Echterhoff (2024) and Itzhak (2024) found LLM framing and anchoring effects comparable to humans. In the Itzhak text read, framing is not tested.
numbers: Mis-citation risk.
limits: Second-hand claim partly wrong.
agent_relevance: Tie every claim to the study actually run.

source: Levin, Schneider, Gaeth (1998) All frames are not created equal: a typology of framing effects
finding: Typology of risky-choice, attribute and goal framing. Support/oppose wording is closest to attribute or goal framing. The Bizer design differs in structure, because it changes resistance to later persuasion.
numbers: Not opened. Known through search snippets and Pinon and Gambara.
limits: Taxonomy only.
agent_relevance: Shows which framing literature applies to the restatement step and which does not.
